analysis.title: Consumer Sentiment Improved Post-Midterm Elections
key_insights: University of Michigan consumer sentiment rose to 51.5 in the final November reading from 51.0 in the initial estimate. The 3.5-point monthly gain pushed the year-over-year growth rate to +1.0%.
The improvement was broad-based. The expectations index rose 4.1 points to 52.9, the highest since July, and the current conditions index rose 2.7 points to 49.4.
One-year-ahead inflation expectations fell to 3.7% in November from 4.7% in October, the lowest since February when the Middle East conflict began. PNC attributes the drop to lower gasoline prices.
Five-year-ahead inflation expectations slipped to 3.3% from 3.5%, on par with February. PNC notes the FOMC watches long-term expectations closely for price stability.
Sentiment diverged by political affiliation. Independents rose 9 points after moving to the left in the midterms, Democrats rose 3.4 points, and Republicans fell 3.1 points.
Sentiment fell in all stock-ownership categories, most for the middle tercile (-2.2 points) and top tercile (-0.9 points). The bottom income tercile fell 0.5 points.
Despite the drop in inflation expectations, consumers said they are more concerned that inflation will cause near-term hardship than that unemployment will rise.
PNC says the sentiment gain may prove temporary. The risks it names are the recent equity sell-off, renewed hostilities in the Middle East, and a government shutdown or debt-ceiling standoff.
